title: How This Hot IPO Is Outfoxing Brazil's Payment Industry Players | Stock News & Stock Market Analysis - IBD

organizations.name: payment industry players | stock news & stock market analysis

text:
Reprints 
Brazil's economy is bouncing back, which is good news for micromerchants such as taxi drivers, physical therapists and food truck operators. It's also good news for PagSeguro ( PAGS ), a payment processor that caters to those individual entrepreneurs and small businesses. 
X Shares in PagSeguro have jumped since its initial public offering in January, the New York Stock Exchange's biggest since Snap ( SNAP ) nearly a year ago, and its IPO raised about $2.27 billion. 
The reason: Some analysts compare PagSeguro to U.S.-based Square ( SQ ), which also focuses on small merchants that are often overlooked by big payment processors. 
"PagSeguro conquered a previously unexplored client base," said Domingos Falavina, a JPMorgan analyst who initiated coverage of the upstart with a neutral rating. "We believe that as first movers, PagSeguro benefited from a positive, contagion effect. Merchants who started accepting cards likely experienced an increase in sales, which drove neighboring merchants to ask for advice on their payment terminal of choice." 
PagSeguro, which provides online and mobile services, sells low-cost payment devices that enable micro-merchants to accept credit or debit cards rather than cash. Analysts estimate that three-fourths of the small businesses who buy PagSeguro's entry-level, mobile point-of-sale device did not accept card payments previously. 
That's similar to Square, which sells those tiny credit-card swipe dongles that plug into smartphones and Apple ( AAPL ) iPads. PagSeguro's "Moderninha" and "Minizinha" devices look like handheld calculators and connect to the internet via Wi-Fi or cellphone networks. Selling Devices Instead Of Leasing 
One key to PagSeguro's success, analysts say, is that the company opted to sell point-of-sale devices to small merchants rather than lease them monthly — which has been the business model of larger rivals such as Cielo and Redecard. 
As Brazil's first payment processor to sell point-of-sale devices, PagSeguro has quickly gained traction in the micro-merchant and small-business market. Small merchants can pay off the device purchases in installments and still afford the payment services that PagSeguro provides. Word-of-mouth marketing should give PagSeguro a boost as Brazil's economy rebounds. 
Economic activity increased in 2017, marking the first expansion in four years. The economy expanded at a faster-than-expected pace in December. Consumer spending has surged due to record-low interest rates, slow inflation and falling unemployment. Brazil's government has focused on deregulation, privatization and deficit-cutting. 
Payment-processing companies owned by Banco Bradesco, Banco do Brasil, Itau Unibanco Holding and Banco Santander Brasil make up more than three quarters of the industry. Cielo, the largest payment processor, is controlled by Bradesco and Banco do Brasil. Redecard is a unit of Itau Unibanco. 
PagSeguro has a different pedigree. PagSeguro is majority owned by Universo Online, Brazil's largest internet portal. Analysts say consumer familiarity with the Universo brand is a plus for PagSeguro. Universo is part of Grupo Folha, the second-largest media conglomerate in the country. 
PagSeguro, as well as its rivals, aim to take advantage as more consumers in Brazil shop online or use credit cards in brick-and-mortar stores. Online shopping accounts for only 3.6% of retail sales vs. 8% in the U.S. and 19% in the U.K., says Morgan Stanley. Card payments in Brazil represent 28% of personal consumption, vs. 45% to 55% in the U.S. and the U.K. Digital Ecosystem 
PagSeguro aims to set itself apart with a digital payments ecosystem, says Jorge Kuri, a Morgan Stanley analyst. 
When merchants sign up with the bank-owned payment firms, they may be pressured to buy other bank-owned products as part of the deal, raising their expenses. Many of PagSeguro's micro-merchant customers, on the other band, may not even have bank accounts. So PagSeguro offers perks. IBD'S TAKE: PagSeguro shares are up by roughly half their IPO price of 21.50. Since going public on Jan. 24, the company already has risen to become the top-ranked stock in IBD's Finance-Credit Card/Payment Processing Group with a Composite Rating of 99. 
"Merchants gain access to more than 30 cash-in methods, business management tools, prepayment of credit-card receivables, accounting reconciliation, and shipping solutions," Kuri said in a note to clients. 
PagSeguro sells its point-of-sale devices at cost; they're not a profit generator. Its high-end Moderninha Pro device costs about $264, which merchants can pay off in 12 installments. That's a bargain compared to the $55 they pay monthly for leasing a top-end Cielo device, Goldman Sachs analyst Carlos Macedo said in a note to clients. 
"Over the last 15 years, the cost for point-of-sale terminals fell by more than 50% in nominal terms," Macedo said. "However, the rental price charged by firms tripled, and the contribution of rental to the bottom line increased to 20% from less than 5%. This was possible because of the relative concentration of the market — the large (payment firms) did not want to upset a highly lucrative business by lowering prices." 
PagSeguro obtains most of its devices from PAX Technology through its local assembler Transire Eletronicos. PAX competes with the likes of VeriFone ( PAY ) and Ingenico. By selling rather than leasing the devices, PagSeguro greatly reduces its own customer acquisition and support costs, Macedo says. Competition Fiercer 
While PagSeguro took was first to target micro-merchants by selling them payment devices rather than leasing them, competition has increased. JPMorgan says others now trying to sell point-of-sale devices include MercadoLibre ( MELI ) subsidiary Mercado Pago, Santander's GetNet, SumUp and iZettle. 
Aside from device sales, PagSeguro garners revenue from transaction fees it charges merchants for processing credit- and debit-card purchases. Those fees are volume-based. 
Most of PagSeguro's profits, like those of other payment processors, come from prepaying a merchant's receivables. Brazil's credit card industry is unusual in that there's a 30-day period to settle transactions vs. two days in the U.S. and other countries. 
PagSeguro uses its own capital to provide merchants with loans covering the value of credit card transactions and collects interest fees on the service. It also uses receivable volume as a guarantee of repayment, analysts say. 
One regulatory risk for the company is that Brazil is mulling a change in financial transaction rules that would shorten the period to settle receivable prepayments with retailers. The government has yet to make a formal proposal. Wall street analysts say the change would be significant but may not come for years. 
PagSeguro's IPO is the first of several in Brazil that may take place in 2018 ahead of presidential elections in October. Drug company Blau; Grupo SBF, owner of sporting goods chain Centauroand; and toy retailer Ri Happy Brinquedos have all filed to go public. YOU MAY ALSO BE INTERESTED IN:
